entries.title: centred header, status badges and section rules
entries.body:
* docs(readme): centred header, status badges and section rules

Restyles the README on the layout amritk/mjst uses: a centred title block
with the tagline and a row of flat-square shields.io badges (status,
licence, TypeScript subset, LLVM 18, Node, wasm targets, the stage2
self-hosting fixpoint, no GC, and the vibe-coded one), horizontal rules
between top-level sections, GitHub alert syntax for the pre-alpha warning,
the build-from-source tip and the unsafe-holes caution, and explicit
alignment markers on every table separator so the columns read the same
way in every renderer.

The pre-alpha note no longer claims the project is untagged — v0.1.0 and
v0.1.1 are out — so it asks for an exact pinned version rather than a
pinned commit. Prose, links and anchors are otherwise untouched;
`node docs/check-links.mjs` passes over all 368 links.

Refs: README.md

* chore(hooks): block tool attribution where a commit is written

CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md have always forbidden session links, tracking IDs,
model names and platform attributions in commits, code and PR text, but a
rule in a document is only as good as the agent reading it: a harness can
inject an instruction of its own to append an agent `Co-Authored-By:`
line, a session-link trailer or a footer naming the tool that wrote the
change, and an agent reading both instructions reads them as compatible.
The mistake is then awkward to fix once pushed and impossible once merged,
so this refuses the tool call rather than restating the rule.

`.claude/hooks/no-attribution.mjs` is a PreToolUse hook over `Bash` and the
GitHub MCP tools. It inspects a command that writes a message into git or
GitHub — `git commit`, `tag`, `merge`, `notes`, `rebase`, `revert`, or any
`gh` command, including the file named by `-F`, `--file`, `--body-file` or
`--template` — and the input of an MCP call that opens or comments on a
pull request or an issue. `Edit`, `Write` and every read-only command are
untouched, so writing documentation about the rule and grepping the history
for offenders both still work. Exit 2 blocks the call and tells the agent
which pattern it hit; unreadable input exits 0, because a hook that cannot
parse what it is fed should not stop a session.

`no-attribution.test.mjs` pins the seven shapes it must block and the eight
it must leave alone — a human's `Co-Authored-By:` trailer among them, and a
repository path that merely looks like a model name.

Tests: .claude/hooks/no-attribution.test.mjs

* fix(hooks): read a tool input as lines, not as one JSON string

Two false positives, both found by the hook refusing a call that was
putting the rule *back*: rewriting the pull request description that
carried the trailers, and a commit whose message named a human co-author.

The GitHub MCP branch scanned `JSON.stringify(toolInput)`, where a body's
newlines are the two characters `\` and `n`, so every pattern anchored to a
line ran to the end of the whole input: a description that merely *named* a
banned trailer, and mentioned `.claude/hooks/` further down, read as one
line carrying both. It now walks the input and scans each string on its
own, and a shell command's literal `\n` is restored before matching, so a
line is a line in either branch.

The co-author pattern then still matched a human's trailer when anything
later on the line said `claude` — `... <p@example.com>" && node
.claude/hooks/...` — because it searched the whole line for a vendor name.
It now reads only the author's name, up to the `<` that opens the address,
plus the address itself when it is at a vendor's own domain.

Both shapes are in the test, which is 17 cases now.

Tests: .claude/hooks/no-attribution.test.mjs

entries.title: add readdirSync, spawnSyncTo and monotonicNanos, and the test runner they enable
entries.body:
* fix(codegen): declare the array header in a module that imports a class with an array field

An importer emits the whole layout of a class it imports, so a field of array
type puts `%struct.Bag = type { %struct.nish_array* }` in that module — but
nothing else there had to mention an array, and the header was never declared.
Both `llvm-as` and clang refuse the result with *use of undefined type named
'struct.nish_array'*, so a class with an array field could not be imported at
all.

`structTypeDeclarations` now declares the header whenever a layout or a
signature it walks mentions an array, in both compilers. It is appended after
the `Result` declarations, so a module that already declared it — for a
signature, or for an array operation in its own code — emits the same bytes it
did before: `addTypeDecl` dedupes by first insertion and these lines come first.

Nothing in the corpus had the shape, because the bug needs an importer that
touches no array of its own: a program that reads `bag.items[0]` declares the
header for the index and hides it. The new case calls a method instead and keeps
every array operation in the exporting module.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#export-and-import
Tests: tests/link/struct_array_field

* feat(std): add std/testing, a test runner written in Nish

`npm test` is Node: `tests/run.js` compiles the corpus, assembles it with
`llvm-as`, links it and diffs stdout against a golden, which needs to spawn a
compiler and read a directory. This is the other half of testing — a compiled
program that checks itself — and it is Nish all the way down, the first module
of a `std/` that did not exist before.

Four language rules shape the API more than any style preference, and each
removes the shape a JavaScript framework would reach for first:

- **A function is not a value**, so there is no `test("name", () => { ... })`. A
  `Suite` is driven by straight-line assertions, with the names as arguments.
- **Every assertion answers a `boolean`**, because a failure cannot throw and be
  collected: an out-of-range index panics and ends the process, so a check that
  a later read depends on has to be a branch —
  `if (!t.eqI32("len", a.length, 3)) { return t.done(); }`.
- **There are no generics**, so there is one assertion per type rather than one
  `eq` that takes strings and loses the type in its message.
- **There are no default parameters**, so each one takes its name and detail in
  full.

The report is the shape this repository's own harness prints — `PASS`, `FAIL`
with an indented detail line, `SKIP  <name> (<reason>)`, and a summary ending
`N passed, M failed, K skipped` — so a skip is counted rather than mentioned,
and `done()` answers the exit code instead of calling `process.exit`, so a
program can run several suites. The widths are spelled `i32` / `i64` / `f64`, so
the module means the same thing under `--number-mode f64` as it does by default.

Source is the distribution format (wp21 §2): an import of a `std/` module
compiles with the program that imports it, and the whole-program attribute pass
sees through it exactly as it sees through the program's own functions. `std/` is
in the package's `files` because a standard library nobody can resolve is not
one; the specifier is relative until WP21 gives the language a bare one.

`std/README.md` also says what this is not — a replacement for `tests/run.js`
needs a directory listing, a child process's output rather than just its status,
and a clock, none of which the language has.

Tests: tests/link/std_testing, tests/link/std_testing_fail

* fix(tests): rewrite builtin calls inside arrow-declared functions

The differential harness rewrites an Nish program into JavaScript and compares
the two byte for byte, mapping each builtin onto `runtime/shim.mjs` so that the
Node side runs this language's semantics rather than JavaScript's. The transform
returned a top-level `const` declaration without visiting its children, which
was right when a top-level `const` was only ever a folded module constant — and
wrong since WP22 made a *function* an arrow bound to one.

So every arrow-declared function body went through unrewritten. A call of
`mkdirSync` stayed a bare `mkdirSync` and threw `ReferenceError` under Node; a
`console.log` stayed JavaScript's own, which is worse, because it prints
something close enough to pass while measuring nothing. Nine whole programs in
the differential corpus are arrow-declared and all nine call a builtin the shim
exists to emulate, `tests/cases/fn_arrow` and `fn_arrow_concise` among them.

No divergence was hiding behind it: with the bodies rewritten the suite still
reports every program agreeing. What was hiding was the comparison itself.

Refs: docs/wp13-differential.md, docs/wp22-arrow-functions.md
Tests: node tests/differential/run.js (146/156 agree, 0 unexpected)

* feat(runtime): add readdirSync, spawnSyncTo and monotonicNanos

Three builtins, and the reason they exist together: a test harness cannot be
written in this language without them. `tests/run.js` discovers its cases,
captures each child's output and times what it ran, and those were the three
things a program the compiler produced could not do.

  readdirSync(path): string[] | null
      the entries, sorted ascending by bytes, without `.` and `..`. Sorted
      because there is no `sort` for a caller to reach for, and because an order
      that is the file system's is an order that differs between two machines
      running the same suite. `null` when the directory cannot be read, which is
      a different answer from the empty array an empty directory gives.
  spawnSyncTo(argv, stdoutPath, stderrPath): number
      `spawnSync` with each stream sent to a file; an empty path leaves that
      stream inherited. A second builtin rather than two more parameters,
      because there are no optional ones — and a file rather than a returned
      string, because the runtime would otherwise have to buffer a child that
      prints more than memory holds, and a harness wants the bytes on disk
      anyway, to diff and to keep after a failure.
  monotonicNanos(): i64
      `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` in nanoseconds. An `i64` in both number modes, because
      `number` is an `i32` by default and overflows inside a tenth of a second.
      Not `readnone`: two reads of a clock that folded into one would make every
      interval measured with them exactly zero.

They cost the runtime 516 bytes of `.text`, all of it in one `static`
implementation that `nish_spawn` now shares, and they cost a program that calls
none of them nothing at all: `examples/hello.ts` at the size profile is
byte-identical against the old runtime and the new. That measurement is now a
test rather than a promise — `node tests/run.js budget` sums every `.text*`
section against a stated ceiling, which had been prose since WP14 and had
drifted from the 2,544 bytes wp7 recorded to 4,088 without anything noticing.

Adding the third one turned up a use-after-free in the second-newest builtin.
`escape.ts` knew that `readFileSync` and `readFileSyncOrNull` bump their result
out of the arena, and did not know it about `getenv`, so a function that
returned a `getenv` result *and* allocated anything locally was given an
automatic arena scope whose `nish_arena_release` ran before the `ret`, rewinding
past the string it was about to return. With `NISH_SCOPE_PROBE=hello` it printed
`value: ZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZZ` after 320 bytes of allocation on top: silent
corruption, shipped in 0.1.0. The list is now a named set with the rule for
extending it written beside it, and `mem_getenv_scope` and `mem_readdir_scope`
pin one case each on top of the `mem_read_or_null_scope` that named the rule.

Measured: 4,670 of 4,864 bytes of `.text*`; +516 for the three, +0 for a program
that calls none
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#directories-and-subprocesses, docs/LANGUAGE.md#the-clock,
docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md, docs/wp7-runtime.md
Tests: tests/cases/io_readdir, io_readdir_null, io_spawn_to,
io_spawn_to_inherit, io_monotonic, mem_getenv_scope, mem_readdir_scope, and six
reject_* cases

* feat(std): add std/text and the golden runner written in Nish

`tests/nish/run.ts` is this repository's golden-case suite, in the language it
tests. It lists `tests/cases` with `readdirSync`, compiles each case by spawning
the compiler, links and runs the ones with a `.out`, diffs the emitted IR against
the golden line by line, reports through a `std/testing` `Suite`, and answers the
exit code. Over the whole corpus it is 598 checks, 0 failed, 5 skipped in about
four and a half minutes: `npm run test:nish`.

The five skips are the sidecars it does not implement (`.env`, `.argv`,
`.stdout`), each named and counted, because a skip that is counted is a to-do
list and one that is not is a green run that proved less than it looks. It is not
a replacement for `tests/run.js` and the difference is worth stating: it covers
the golden cases and none of the pipeline checks — no interop sidecars, no layout
assertions, no wasm profiles, no packaging, no self-hosting oracles, and none of
the fourteen flag variations parity runs. What it demonstrates is that the
language can host a harness; what `tests/run.js` does is prove the compiler.

`npm test` builds it and runs it over the `pop` cases — one golden, one native
round trip, three rejections, 2.4 seconds — rather than over the corpus, because
it spawns a compiler per case and a second full pass would double the suite to
prove what those five prove. It is also the only place `readdirSync`,
`spawnSyncTo` and `monotonicNanos` are exercised together on a real workload
rather than in a case written to pin one rule.

Writing it needed two things of the standard library. `std/text` is the first:
`splitLines`, `splitWhitespace`, `trim` and its halves, `contains`, `replaceAll`
and `firstDifference` over two arrays of lines. The language has no `split`, no
`trim` and no regular expression — each allocates and some need a character table
the runtime has no room for — so a program that reads a file and wants its lines
writes the loop, and this is that loop written once. `replaceAll` collects its
parts and `join`s them rather than concatenating in the loop, which is the shape
this project has measured the cost of: 180 MB of peak arena for 88 KB of output.

Two things the runner had to learn that say something about the harness it
mirrors: a `-g` golden holds `producer: "nish <version>"` rather than the real
version, so a release commit is not red at itself, and the goldens fold the
absolute repository root to `<root>` because `tests/run.js` compiles with absolute
paths. The runner compiles with relative ones — there is no `cwd` builtin to
build an absolute path from — so it folds the placeholder out of the golden
instead. Both were found by running it over the corpus and reading what
disagreed, which is also how it found that `str_f64_mode` needs the per-case
`<name>.c` driver rather than `tests/driver.c`.

Tests: tests/link/std_text (65 assertions through `Suite`), and the `pop` subset
in the WP8-adjacent section of tests/run.js

entries.title: fix the install links and record the npm name conflict
entries.body:
The first binary release made three sets of documentation false at once, and
all three were things a new user would hit before anything else.

**The install commands 404ed.** `docs/INSTALL.md` §2 told readers to `curl`
`releases/download/v0.1.0/nish-0.1.0-x86_64-linux.tar.gz` and to
`npm install -g ./nish-0.1.0.tgz`. There is no v0.1.0 release: the tag was
pushed by a workflow using the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`, GitHub raises no event
for that, and nothing ever built it — which is the bug v0.1.1 exists to fix.
Both commands now name **v0.1.1**, the one release there is, and the `.tgz` is
fetched rather than assumed to be lying in the working directory. The URLs are
version-pinned rather than using `/releases/latest/download/`, because that
form needs the asset's exact file name and both asset names carry the version
in them; the paragraph says so, so the next reader does not re-derive it.

**`npm install -g nish` installs somebody else's package.** The name on the
public registry has belonged to `stdarg`'s "A Node.js Interactive shell" since
February 2014 — 0.0.0 and 0.0.1, both deprecated by their author with the
message `It was a bad idea`, nothing published since, last touched 2022-06-21.
This was written in three places as though it were our name, so it is
corrected in all three: `INSTALL.md` §2, `wp12-release.md`'s manual-publish
step, and `wp19-stage0-retirement.md` G5, whose "`npm install -g nish` keeps
working" bullet assumed a name we do not have. `wp12-release.md` gains an
**Open decision: the npm name is taken** section with the registry facts, a
one-line command to re-verify them, and the three options — a scope such as
`@amritk/nish`, a different bare name, or npm's dispute process — with what
each costs. No name is chosen here: the name reaches `package.json`,
`bin.nish`, `release.yml` and, if the binary is to match, both `branding.ts`
files, so it is the repository owner's decision and not a docs sweep's.

**The benchmark gap count no longer matches the table.** `MASTER_PLAN.md`
said in two places that four of the seven benchmarks miss the 1.10x target.
`BENCHMARKS.md` shows one — fib at 1.15x against Rust `-O3`, which the same
suite re-measures at 261 ms against Rust's 262 when the runs are interleaved,
so it is run-to-run spread rather than the program. Both places now match the
table and cite `wp9-optimisation.md` §Summary, which had already been
corrected. `wp24-async.md` carried the same stale count in its threads
section and is corrected with them; `wp15-performance.md` did not.

Found while sweeping, and fixed here because it is the same drift:
`wp12-release.md` counted 134 packed files at 0.1.0 (it is 146 at 0.1.1) and
sized `self/` at 54 modules and 791,835 bytes (it is 58 and 944,676, which
moves the "ship `self/`" row's unpacked estimate from 2.1 MB to 2.4 MB);
`wp19-stage0-retirement.md` G3 and R2 still said the bootstrap job has no seed
"until 0.1.0 ships", when v0.1.1 shipped one; and `README.md`'s quickstart was
the most visible copy of the wrong `npm install` line of all.

`docs/BENCHMARKS.md` still reports `nish 0.0.0` in its header, and is
deliberately left alone: it is generated, hand-editing a header is how a table
starts claiming a run it did not come from, and regenerating it needs a quiet
machine. `bench/README.md` now explains the line instead — the header
describes the run, the run predates the version bump, and nothing in `src/`,
`self/`, `runtime/` or `bench/` has changed since it, so the numbers are still
the current compiler's.

entries.title: give every thread its own arena behind `--threads`
entries.body:
WP20 T0, the one stage of the threading plan that has no language surface.

The arena's fast path is not a call into C: `src/codegen/runtime.ts` emits
an `alwaysinline` IR function that GEPs `@nish_arena` and bumps it with a
plain non-atomic load/add/store, and every `new`, object literal, array
literal and string concatenation goes through it. Two threads allocating
is therefore a data race **in the emitted IR**, which no amount of care in
`runtime.c` could have fixed. `--threads` fixes it where it lives.

What the flag changes is one line:

```llvm
@nish_arena = external thread_local(initialexec) global %struct.nish_arena, align 8
```

Nothing else moves. LLVM 18 accepts a thread-local global straight in the
allocator's GEP operand, so the `alwaysinline` body is the same text either
way and `@llvm.threadlocal.address` is not needed; on x86-64 the fast path
gains one `movq nish_arena@GOTTPOFF(%rip)` and then addresses all three
fields off `%fs`. `initialexec` is named rather than defaulted so that a
`-fPIC` build — the `napi` profile, which is the host that will want this —
does not lower an allocation to a `__tls_get_addr` call.

On the C side, `runtime/runtime.c`, `runtime/nish.h` and
`runtime/runtime_wasm.c` each define the same `NISH_TLS` macro, empty unless
`-DNISH_THREADS`, and it sits on `nish_arena` and on the `Math.random` seed
word. `nish_argv` deliberately does not take it: it is written once before
the program runs and read-only afterwards, and the reason is now written
beside it rather than assumed. `scripts/build.sh --threads` passes the macro
and the matching `-ftls-model=initial-exec`, and `nish --threads --link`
passes the flag on, so the two halves of a build move together — and cannot
quietly fail to, because ELF refuses a non-TLS reference to a TLS definition.
A mismatched pair is a link error, and that is pinned as a check rather than
left to luck.

With the flag off nothing moved at all: no golden `.ll` changed, `runtime.c`
is the same number of bytes of `.text*` — the suite's `RUNTIME_TEXT_BUDGET`
gate measures exactly that build and did not move — and `examples/hello.ts` is
the same binary byte for byte. That is what makes T0 landable before the 1.0
freeze while the rest of WP20 cannot be.

What it costs when a program does ask is in the table in the note. The short
version is that the thread pointer costs about half again on a loop that does
nothing but bump, and nothing measurable on real programs, because no real
program's hot loop is the allocator.

No program can start a thread yet, and nothing here lets one: the language
surface is still WP20 T1 to T4 and still 1.1 scope. What this unblocks is a
*host* starting one — a C driver, or the `napi_create_async_work` shim
wp24-async.md §5.1 asked for, whose whole cost was this.

Measured: runtime.c `.text*` at -Oz unchanged to the byte, 4,670 of its 4,864
budget with the flag off (4,795 with it, still inside, and an opt-in build
nobody links without asking); examples/hello.ts byte-identical at 4,680; 1.48x
on an allocation-bound loop with the flag on, against 1.00x on bench/strbuild
and 1.03x on bench/nbody

entries.title: measure a -g position from the declaration, and its column in bytes
entries.body:
* fix(codegen): measure a -g position from the declaration, and its column in bytes

`node tests/run.js --parity` was red on `main`, on two independent `-g`
defects that no oracle could see. Both were stage0's, and both are fixed
here.

**A function's position is its declaration, not its arrow.** With `-g`,
`export const add = (a: i32, b: i32): i32 => a + b` was described from the
`ArrowFunction`, whose own start is its parameter list — so stage0 put `add`
at column 20 where stage1, whose parser normalises both spellings into one
node spanning the declaration, put it at column 1. The same function got two
different positions depending on which of WP22's two spellings declared it,
which is exactly the identity stage A was declared done on; under `-g` it had
not held since arrows landed. It reached the line as well as the column:
when the arrow sits below its `const`, the `DISubprogram`, its `scopeLine`
and every parameter's `DILocalVariable` all named the arrow's line. A
debugger asked where `add` is declared should answer where a reader would say
it is, and the answer may not depend on the spelling.

The fix is `FunctionSig.declSite`, recorded by the checker and read by
`debug.ts` — the node the declaration begins at, which is `decl` itself for a
`function`, a method and a constructor, and the `VariableStatement` for the
arrow form. It is recorded rather than re-derived because the emitter may not
climb to a parent to find out what a node is part of, which is the same
resolution PR #41 reached for the concise body.

**A `DILocation` column counts bytes.** The run that proved the arrow fix came
back with ten undeclared differences still standing, one cause between them
and nothing to do with arrows: `self/checker.ts:1305` has an em dash inside a
warning string, and stage0 counted the UTF-16 code units the `typescript` API hands it where
stage1 counts bytes. `clang -g` settles it — it puts the `return` after a
three-byte em dash at column 13, the byte count, where code units say 11. A
DWARF column is read back against the file's bytes, and the language already
measures a string's `length` in bytes. Stage0's *diagnostic* columns are
deliberately untouched and stay code units: the consumer there is an editor.

Stage1 needed no code change for either — its parser normalises, and every
offset in `self/` is already a byte offset — so it gains the two comments
that say why, and the corpus dumps shift by those lines.

**Why a closed gate could reopen in silence.** An empty difference set is a
fact about the corpus, not about the language: every `-g` case was written in
the `function` spelling, and every one of them was ASCII, so 8,358 runs never
posed either question. `--parity` is a mode rather than a section of `npm
test`, so nothing on the way to `main` asks. `tests/cases/dbg_arrow` and
`tests/cases/dbg_utf8` close both holes, and `docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md`
§A5 corrects R1/G1's "empty difference set" and costs running the mode in CI.

Measured: parity 8708 runs over 622 programs, 0 undeclared differences (1617 declared)
Refs: docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md#a5
Tests: tests/cases/dbg_arrow, tests/cases/dbg_utf8

* docs(self): record the parity run against current main in §A5

The green run §A5 quotes was measured against 045c8f8. `main` has moved twice
since — #49 and #55 — and #55's `--threads` is a fifteenth flag variation, so
the cross product is 9,345 runs over 623 programs rather than 8,708 over 622.
The difference set is still empty and the declarations are still §A4's five.

Re-measured on the merged tree, which is the only number worth quoting: a gate
whose whole lesson is that an old measurement reads as a current one should not
carry an old measurement.

Measured: parity 9345 runs over 623 programs, 0 undeclared differences (1669 declared)
Refs: docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md#a5

entries.title: give every symbol a package scope
entries.body:
The whole-program fact table was keyed by a bare name, so two packages that
each kept a private `helper()` could not be compiled into one program:
whichever was collected second would have been handed the first one's purity,
escape and pointer facts, and that is a miscompile rather than a link error.
`Compilation` refused such a program outright, and that refusal was the one
hard blocker in front of a package ecosystem ([wp21-packages.md](docs/wp21-packages.md) §5a).

Symbols are package-scoped now. A module belongs to exactly one package, every
function, method and constructor it declares is emitted under
`<prefix><name>`, and the fixpoint is keyed by that symbol — so a name is
never a key again.

**The root package's prefix is empty**, and that asymmetry is the whole design.
The plan offered `pkg@version.symbol` or a content hash; both qualify the
program's own code as readily as a dependency's, so both move every symbol in
every program — rewriting every golden `.ll`, every `--emit-header` asm label
and the three interop sidecars to buy nothing at all for the single-package
programs that are the only programs that exist today. With an empty root prefix
a program of one package emits byte for byte the IR it always did: not one of
the 182 checked-in goldens moved, no exported name moved, and no C ABI changed.
A prefix appears only where a second package does, which is a program that did
not compile at all before.

Which package a module is in is read off the module name the compiler already
carries — a module under `node_modules/<name>/` is in that package, everything
sharing the entry's own package directory is the root package — so there is no
manifest, no resolver, no flag and no language surface. It is the same string
in both compilers, so stage0 and stage1 agree without stage1 growing a working
directory it has no room for. The rule is a placeholder for the one WP21 S2's
resolver will state, and both files say so in a `TODO(WP21 S2)`.

S1 stops at functions on purpose. A class is still one `%struct.<name>` for the
whole program and type equality still compares names, so two packages that each
declare `Node` are now *reported*, naming both packages, rather than silently
sharing one layout. Scoping struct identity — and saying what a `Point` from
two versions of one package means — is §7's question.

Mirrored in `self/`, which is the largest program the scheme had to survive:
`self/packages.ts` is the new module, and `tests/self/ir_oracle.js` compiles
the corpus with both compilers and diffs the IR byte for byte, the new
two-package program included.

entries.title: read a numeric `enum` as a distinct `i32` type
entries.body:
`enum Kind { If = 1, While = 2 }` was `Only top-level function declarations are
supported in Phase 1 (found EnumDeclaration)`. It is a declaration now, in
stage0 and stage1 alike, and Phase 0 keeps every refusal it had: a member whose
initialiser is not a numeric literal is still `Enum members must be numeric
literals`.

**An enum is a distinct type whose representation is `i32`** — stricter than
TypeScript, where a numeric enum member is assignable to `number`. It has to
be: the rule this language is built on is that two values are compatible only
when their types are identical, so an enum that were silently `i32` would be
the one type compatible with something it is not spelled as. `Kind` and `i32`
are two types in both directions, and the only values of `Kind` are the members
it declares.

There is no lowering, and that is the point. A member is folded the way a
module constant is, so `Kind.While` is the literal `2`, a `Kind` parameter is
an `i32` parameter, and the `switch` a discriminant exists for is the jump
table it has always been. `tests/cases/enum_ir.ts` and `enum_expanded.ts` are
one program written twice — with the enum, and with `i32` module constants —
and their `.ll` goldens are byte-identical files; if they ever differ, an enum
has started to cost something. No golden that existed before this change moved.

What distinctness forces was decided rather than inherited. **`switch` takes an
enum discriminant and enum-member labels**, because a `switch` over a
discriminant is what an enum is worth; `case 1:` on one is `` `case` label is
i32 but the discriminant is Kind ``, so the integer a member stands for is not
the member. **Bit flags stay `i32` module constants**: `|` on an enum would
produce a value that is no declared member, and refusing it is the only one of
the three answers wp23 §10 lists that can be widened later without
invalidating a program already written. `biome.json` turns `noEnum` off for the
Nish-program half and leaves it an error over `src/`.

Two rules follow the `type` alias that landed before this. Auto-numbering is
TypeScript's — a member with no initialiser is the one before it plus one, from
`0` — and an enum cannot be exported, for the alias's reason: a module's
signatures are resolved before its imports are bound, so an imported name in
type position resolves provisionally as a class, and an enum has no layout to
stand in for. `const enum` is refused by name in *both* compilers rather than
by stage1's grammar, so the two report it byte for byte identically; `declare
enum` is stage0's rule and stage1's parser refuses the same file as a syntax
error, which is the class `tests/self/parity.js` already declares.

stage1 grows the grammar to match: `enum` stays a contextual keyword matched by
text where `type`, `from` and `of` are, so the lexer and its oracle are
untouched; `N_ENUM` is node kind 59 and `N_ENUM_MEMBER` 60, `K_ENUM` is type
kind 16, and `tests/parser_oracle.js` transcribes `EnumDeclaration` into them so
the two parsers are still compared node for node. `-g` describes an enum as
DWARF's `DW_TAG_enumeration_type` with one `DIEnumerator` per member, so a
debugger prints `While` rather than `2`. Nish-0, the subset `self/` is itself
written in, is unchanged: `self/` keeps its 171 module constants until the
bootstrap seed policy lets it convert them.

entries.title: add slice, a string cut that checks instead of clamping
entries.body:
`s.slice(start[, end])` joins `substring` as the second of the two string
slices WP15 §4 asks for. `substring` keeps JavaScript's clamp, so a program
ported from TypeScript behaves the way its author expects; `slice` requires
`0 <= start <= end <= s.length` and panics otherwise, so what it lowers to is
two `icmp ule` against a cold `nish_panic_slice` block, one `getelementptr`
and one `nish_str_new` — `substring`'s six `llvm.smin` / `llvm.smax` calls,
gone. Two compares are the whole range test, because a negative offset
sign-extends to a value above any byte length; with no `end`, `end` *is* `len`
and only the ordering compare is emitted. `--unchecked-indexing` drops both,
as it drops `a[i]`'s.

**The name is `slice`, not the `sliceFast` / `subarray` that section proposed.**
Both of those are `TS2339: Property '...' does not exist on type 'string'`
under `tsc --strict`, and the rule `wp23-language-surface.md` §7 declines
`for...of` over a string to protect is that an Nish program is a TypeScript
program `tsc --strict` also accepts. A method nobody else has breaks that
harder than a loop that means something else, because it does not even
compile. `slice` is in `lib.es5.d.ts` with the right signature, and for an
in-range, non-negative pair it answers exactly what JavaScript answers. What
it does not reproduce is JavaScript's argument handling — a negative offset
counted from the end, `""` for a reversed pair — which is the same shape of
divergence `charCodeAt` already carries by panicking where JavaScript answers
`NaN`, and is written down the same way.

The other half of the case is not the instruction count. A check is provable
and a clamp is not: `tests/cases/str_slice` slices constant offsets out of a
literal and `opt -O2` deletes every compare, branch and panic block in the
module, which no optimiser can do to a clamp that is part of the answer rather
than a test that might be redundant. That is why the two live side by side
instead of one replacing the other, and it is what the ranged types of §2.1
compound.

`nish_panic_slice` is a new runtime symbol rather than a reuse of
`nish_panic_index`: a reversed pair is as common a mistake as an end past the
string, and `index out of range: i >= len` describes neither. It costs 113
bytes of `.text` at `-Oz`, spent under §7's rule on the measurement below.
metrics: 1.18x on a lexer-shaped scan (734 ms to 618 ms, min of 20 alternating runs), and 8.3% fewer instructions retired whole-program under callgrind (339,516,079 to 313,516,079) — 13 x86-64 instructions per slice

entries.title: assert the seed equality only when the seed is stage0
entries.body:
`scripts/bootstrap.sh --verify` asserted three equalities whatever the seed
was, and one of them means two different things depending on what the seed
is.

With **stage0** as the seed, `IR(seed) == IR(stage1)` says that two
independently written implementations of the same source revision emit the
same IR for it: `src/` in TypeScript and `self/` in Nish, agreeing byte for
byte. That is the second half of Wheeler's diverse double-compiling, it is
the strongest thing this repository asserts, and it is unchanged here.

With a **released binary** as the seed — which is what CI's `bootstrap (from
the last release)` job passes — the same comparison says something else
entirely: that the IR this working tree emits for `self/` is the IR the last
release emitted for it. That is one implementation at two points in time. It
is not a bootstrap property at all; it is a freeze on codegen between
releases, and it fails on exactly the changes a release cycle exists to
carry. It failed that way the first time one landed: a flow-sensitive bounds
analysis proved 46 of `self/`'s 1,206 index checks redundant, 20 of 56
modules changed, and the seeded job reported a broken bootstrap because an
optimisation had worked — while the fixed point held over all 56 modules and
stage3 stayed byte-identical to stage2.

So the seed equality is now asserted for a stage0 seed and reported for any
other, in a note that says at length that it is not a failure.
`IR(stage1) == IR(stage2)` and `stage3 == stage2` are properties of the
working tree alone and stay asserted whatever the seed is.

The seed is identified rather than inferred from the variable: naming this
checkout's own `dist/index.js` in `NISH_BOOTSTRAP` is stage0 spelled a second
way, and keeps stage0's equalities, so the spelling the script's own header
recommends does not silently drop the strongest line in the file.

What the seeded run enforces is the rolling freeze — "a construct added in
0.N cannot be used by `self/` until 0.(N+1)" — and it enforces it by stage1
being built at all: a `self/` reaching for something the seed has never heard
of does not compile and never reaches a comparison. That failure now names
the rule it broke instead of leaving the reader the compiler's diagnostic and
no context.

`tests/self/bootstrap.js`, which `npm test` runs, seeds with stage0 and keeps
asserting all three.

entries.title: pin every diagnostic wording a program can provoke
entries.body:
* test(self): pin every diagnostic wording a program can provoke

A diagnostic code is a promise about a rule; the sentence behind it is not
promised, but until stage0 is deleted it is *proved*, by two implementations
printing the same words. After R6 it would be proved by nothing. That is the
half of gate G2.4 `docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md` §2B calls the wording gap,
and R3 calls "the half that matters".

**The gap is now a command rather than a number.**
`tests/diagnostic_coverage.js` reads the registry out of `self/codes.ts` — the
half that outlives stage0 — compiles the negatives, the `perf_*` positives and
the new `tests/wordings/` corpus, and reads the `code` field of every `--json`
object. It never matches the compiler's source against a table copied out of
it, which is the only way the measurement still means something after `src/`
is gone.

Run first, it said the gap was **176 uncovered of 351 codes**, not the 196 of
344 the note recorded: seven codes and twenty-seven covered wordings had
landed in between. A number in a document goes stale; this one can be
recomputed with `--report`.

`tests/wordings/` closes it. 117 small programs, each named for the code it
pins (`nl2200_empty_import_list.ts`), with the whole message in its `.err`. A
reword fails twice over — the message no longer matches, and
`scripts/gen-diagnostic-codes.mjs` gives the new words a new number, so the
code no longer matches either. Under `--require-coverage` the tool refuses to
go green while any registry code is neither provoked nor named in
`tests/wordings/unreachable.txt` with a reason, so the next diagnostic arrives
with a case or with a sentence. Coverage is 298 of 351, and the other 53 are
unreachable.

**Those 53 are a finding about the compiler, not a test nobody wrote**: 23
retired fragments the generator keeps for their numbers, 12 that are not
diagnostics at all (the driver's `console.error` usage errors and the
`fail(...)` helper that writes the N-API shim's *generated* C both match the
generator's scan, so `--json` can never carry those codes), 11 preempted by
Phase 0 or by a nearer rule, four shadowed by a longer fragment of their own
message, and three structurally impossible.

**Writing a program per code asked the two compilers a question no oracle
asks**, for the reason §A2 gives about flags: every oracle compiles the
programs that are checked in, and none of these was. 44 of the 117 are §A3's
declared parser class, and those wordings go with stage0 at R6. Eleven are not
declared anywhere: five refuse with a different sentence — two of them with no
code at all — and **six stage1 compiles outright**, including an `i64` and a
`u64` literal past 2^53 and `new Point<i32>()` with its type arguments
ignored. Nothing is fixed here, because a code is keyed on its message text
and rewording one retires the code; both lists are checked in and shrink-only,
and `npm test` runs the tool over stage1 with `--strict-refusals` so a case
that starts agreeing fails until its line is deleted.

The sequential `--json` loop this replaces in `tests/run.js` spawned a
compiler per `reject_*` case, 252 of them, one at a time; the tool pools them
the way the oracles already pool theirs, and walks the `tests/link/` negatives
as well — which is where the uncoded backlog of 1 turns out to be 5, four
whole-program rules that never had a code and that nothing was counting.

Measured: 176 registry codes provoked by nothing before, 0 after (298 covered, 53 unreachable); 392 programs in 5 m 41 s through stage0 and 2.4 s through stage1, against 252 compiled one at a time by the loop it replaces
Refs: docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md
Tests: tests/wordings, tests/diagnostic_coverage.js

* Merge origin/main into wp19/diagnostic-wording

Brings in #57 (package-scoped symbols), #54 (numeric enums) and #53 (the
fast slice) on top of the #49/#55/#60 merges already on this branch.

Nothing conflicted. **But this branch's deliverable is a claim about the
registry, and the registry has grown three times while it waited**, so the
claim was re-derived with the branch's own tool rather than carried
forward. `--require-coverage` found four real failures, all of them the
drift the gate exists to catch:

  nl2226_export_enum: expected NL2226, got NL2288
  NL2123 is provoked by nothing
  NL2226 is provoked by nothing
  NL2286 is provoked by nothing
  NL2287 is provoked by nothing

Resolved case by case, from what the compiler does rather than from what
the note says:

- **`nl2226_export_enum` -> `nl2288_export_enum`.** WP23 gave the exported
  enum a rule of its own, so the case pins `NL2288` now. Renamed and
  re-pinned.
- **`NL2226` is still live**, and needed a case rather than an excuse: the
  catch-all for `export` on a statement that is neither function, class,
  interface nor constant is reached by `export import A = require(...)`
  (an `ImportEqualsDeclaration`). New case `nl2226_export_import_equals`.
- **`NL2286`** (`declare enum`) is reachable and had no case. New case
  `nl2286_declare_enum`.
- **`NL2123`** is the `case` label rule as it was worded before WP23
  admitted an enum member; `NL2284` supersedes it. Retired, with the
  reason on file.
- **`NL2287`** ("An enum member name must be an identifier") has no source
  site in either compiler and never had one -- WP23 reserved the number
  and no message produces the fragment. Retired, with that said plainly.

`parser_refusals.txt` moves both ways, which is what it is for: the two
new cases join it (stage1's parser refuses `export import` and
`declare enum` before the phase that owns the rule can state them), and
`nl2226_export_enum` leaves it -- WP23 put the enum rule in *both*
compilers, so stage1 now answers `export enum` with the same sentence
stage0 does. 44 -> 45.

**Re-derived, and these are the numbers the prose now carries:**

    stage0: 119/119 cases pin their code, coverage 307/362 codes,
            55 unreachable, uncoded=5
    stage1: 63/119 cases pin their code (45 refused by the parser,
            11 answered differently), coverage 214/362, uncoded=7

**Five or six was settled by running them, not by trusting either text.**
§2B said six programs stage0 refuses that stage1 compiles and listed six;
the R3 row said five. Compiling all eleven declared divergences with
stage1 and reading the exit status: **six** compile (`nl2054_literal_u64`,
`nl2055_literal_i64`, `nl2134_for_of_two_variables`, `nl2206_generic_new`,
`nl2241_for_of_initializer`, `nl2242_for_of_annotation`) and five refuse
with a different sentence. §2B was right; the R3 row is corrected.

The §5 table also gains one clause: R1's "empty difference set" was
recorded while it was not true, so the row now points at §A5, which #60
added as the correction.

Refs: docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md
Tests: node tests/diagnostic_coverage.js --require-coverage

entries.title: store an array of records contiguously
entries.body:
WP15 §2a. An array whose element type is a **record** — an `interface`
nobody `implements` — is now one block of structs, `N` of them end to end at
exactly the stride and alignment clang gives the matching C array, instead of
one pointer per slot into wherever the arena happened to put each element.
`ps[i]` is an interior `getelementptr` and *is* the element: no pointer to
load, nothing to chase, and two adjacent records on one cache line. A C host
reads `((struct Point *)a->data)[i]` with no marshalling, and `--emit-header`
says so above each prototype.

**What a record is, and why that is narrower than the plan said.** The plan
said "arrays of structs". The language has two struct kinds and only one can
take value semantics without changing what the language means. An `interface`
is fields and nothing else — no constructor, no methods, no `this` — so
copying one into a slot cannot be told apart from pointing at it. A `class`
has identity: a constructor runs on one object, a method mutates the `this` it
was handed, and every other position in the language passes a class value by
reference. An interface some class `implements` is not a record either — that
array is the language's only polymorphic container, a `Shape[]` holding a
`Square` and a `Circle`, and both are longer than `Shape`.

The class half is not a judgement call, it is measured on the largest Nish
program there is. `self/` keeps one `FunctionSig` in `program.functions`, in
`StructInfo.methodSigs` and in `StructInfo.ctor` at once and writes
`sig.poisoned` through whichever it has to hand; `declareStruct` registers a
`StructInfo` and goes on filling in the object the registry now holds. A
stage1 built with class arrays as value slots rejects `self/` with 41 errors
of the form "`Field ctor of class StructInfo` has no initializer and no
constructor assigns it" — the registry handing back a copy whose constructor
never ran. Every registry in that compiler is built that way, so contiguous
*class* arrays are a migration, not a layout change, and §2a records it as its
own item.

**The rule that makes the layout safe.** An element reference may not be held
across a mutation of the array it came from (`NL2280`). `push` may move the
block and `pop` hands the slot back to the next `push`, so a `const` bound to
`a[i]` or `a.pop()`, or the variable of a `for (const p of a)`, is invalid
after either — or after a call handed that array as a non-`readonly`
parameter, since whether the callee pushes is a whole-program question this
phase does not answer. A loop is checked as a whole, because a `push` at the
bottom of the body reaches a reference taken at the top on the next pass, and
`ps.push(ps[i])` has a message of its own (`NL2281`): the argument is read
after the growth has already abandoned the block. The analysis is
`codegen/escape.ts`'s, run in the phase that is allowed to report.

Two attribute claims moved with the layout, both in the safe direction. A
record pointer may now be an interior element at `i * sizeof(P)`, so `align 8`
would be a lie for a record whose size is not a multiple of eight; the
record's own alignment is what is emitted instead, and only for record types.
And a push or an element store into a record array *copies*, so the value is
read rather than captured — which is what lets an object built only to be
stored become an entry-block alloca the `memcpy` reads from.

Both compilers, mirrored, with the bootstrap still at its fixed point:
`IR(stage0) == IR(stage1) == IR(stage2)`, stage3 byte-identical to stage2 over
55 modules. `runtime.c` needed no code change — `nish_array_grow` and
`nish_alloc_array` have always taken `elem_size` — but its documentation and
`nish.h`'s did, and the layout smoke test now hands C a grown `P[]` to walk
through a matching `struct P *`, checking the stride and every field of every
element. `runtime.c` stays at 4,088 bytes of `.text` at `-Oz`, inside its
4,096-byte budget.

**Read the second and third rows of the measurement before quoting the
first.** A bump allocator lays objects out in allocation order, so an array
built and then walked in the same order was already contiguous underneath and
the pointer load costs nothing the out-of-order core cannot hide; and an
L2-resident working set does not care either. The win is what happens the
moment allocation order and traversal order differ, which is what any program
that builds two arrays in one loop does.

| Shape (x86-64, LLVM 18, `--profile speed --number-mode f64`, min of 7) | pointers | records | |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 200k records, a second array built in the same loop, 2000 passes | 1864 ms | 820 ms | **2.27x** |
| 1M records built in traversal order, 200 passes | 588 ms | 579 ms | 1.02x |
| 8192 records, `d.x = s.x * 2.0` elementwise, 150k passes | 1501 ms | 1500 ms | none |

`bench/nbody` and `bench/vec3` are unchanged, and deliberately: their `Body`
and `Vec3` are classes with constructors, which is exactly the half of §2a
this does not do.
metrics: 2.27x on a record loop whose allocation order differs from its traversal order

entries.title: compile generic functions by monomorphisation
entries.body:
A function may declare type parameters now, in either spelling, and every
instantiation is compiled to its own specialised function: one `define` per
(template, type-argument tuple), named by appending `$` and each argument's
mangled type to the template's name. There is no boxing, no type dictionary and
no runtime type information left in the binary — `identity<i32>` is
`@identity$i32`, and its IR is the IR of the monomorphic function somebody would
have written by hand with the symbol renamed. `tests/run.js` checks that
equality rather than asserting it: it compiles a generic and its hand-written
twin and compares the two `define` blocks byte for byte.

Three decisions carry the change, and each is what keeps it small.

**A type parameter is never a type.** A template's annotations are left as
syntax and resolved once per instantiation with `T` bound in the checker's
named-type resolver, so nothing was added to `StaticType` or to stage1's
`TypeTable` and no pass below the signature level has a type variable to
handle. Inference is unification over annotation *shapes* against argument
types — `T` against `i32`, `T[]` against `i32[]`, `Result<T, string>` against
`Result<i32, string>` — left to right, first binding wins. Type arguments are
therefore never written at a call site, which is also what one token of
lookahead can parse: `f<i32>(x)` and `(f < i32) > (x)` are the same three
tokens, and both compilers now recognise that shape and name the rule.

**One AST, N type assignments.** `identity`'s `return x;` is one node with two
types, so each instantiation owns a copy of the node-keyed side tables and the
five passes that walk a body — the checker, the escape analysis, the attribute
fixpoint, the emitter and the `--emit-checked` dump — install them around the
function they are walking. That is `docs/wp18-generics.md` §3d's overlay with
the tables swapped rather than put behind an accessor, so no read site changed.
Facts fall out per instantiation for free, because they were always keyed by
symbol: `eq<T>` is `readnone` at `T = i32` and `readonly` at `T = string`.

**Termination is a rule, not a number.** An instantiation that asks for one of
the same template whose type argument strictly contains its own has put that
argument under a constructor, and the chain has no end; it is refused by name,
with the concrete chain in the message. Recursion that passes the parameter on
or binds it to a ground type is accepted and drains, so `countDown<string>`
asking for `countDown<i32>` is two instantiations and no more. Behind the rule
are two compiler limits whose message says they are limits.

`Result<T, E>` and `Array<T>` stay built-in, as §6.1 decided: a type argument
is an ordinary type, so `Result<T, string>` as a parameter and `T = i32[]`
both work with no special case. Generic classes, constraints, the whole-program
rule and the peripheries are not in this change; §16 of the note is the order
to take them in, and each is refused today with a message that says which one
it is waiting for. `self/` implements generics and does not use them, so the
bootstrap is a control: byte-identical IR over an unchanged `self/`, before and
after.

Measured: 732 -> 2,985 bytes of `.text` at `--profile size` for one template at
1, 2, 4 and 8 type arguments, and `IR(stage0) == IR(stage1)` byte for byte over
every new case
Refs: docs/wp18-generics.md#15-what-landed, docs/LANGUAGE.md#generic-functions
Tests: tests/cases/gen_identity, gen_eq_purity, gen_infer_two,
gen_recursive_ground, gen_result_payload, reject_generic_function,
reject_generic_polymorphic_recursion, reject_generic_call_type_args,
reject_generic_dollar_name, reject_generic_constraint, reject_generic_arity,
reject_generic_method, reject_generic_class, reject_type_alias_generic

entries.title: split the system-call half into runtime_os.c, with a ceiling each
entries.body:
* ci: run the golden cases through the Nish runner on every pull request

`npm test` builds `tests/nish/run.ts` and runs it over five cases, which proves
the runner compiles and works. Only the full pass proves it still *agrees* with
the goldens, and that pass has so far only ever run by hand — which is how a
harness rots.

It is not a duplicate of the `test` job, and what it adds is worth stating: a
compiler regression fails in both, but a regression in the runner itself, or in
`readdirSync`, `spawnSyncTo` or `monotonicNanos` — which nothing else exercises
together on a real workload — fails only here. The job runs in parallel with
`test`, so it costs a runner rather than wall-clock time, and it spawns a
compiler per case, which is why `npm test` still does not pay for it.

`set -o pipefail` in the step is load-bearing rather than decoration: the default
shell for a `run:` step is `bash -e` without it, so the exit status of
`npm run test:nish | tee` would be `tee`'s, and a runner answering 1 would have
been a green step.

* test: guard the two classes behind the getenv and arrow-rewrite bugs

Both bugs fixed in #47 were the same shape — a list that had to be kept in step
with another list, and was not — and in both the symptom was invisible rather
than loud. Fixing the instances does not stop the next one, so these two guards
derive the property instead of restating the list.

**Every allocating builtin is an allocation site.** `escape.ts` gives a function
an automatic arena scope only when nothing it returns is fresh arena memory, so a
builtin missing from `ALLOCATING_BUILTINS` gets its result released before the
`ret` — the use-after-free `getenv` shipped with. The guard asks each of the 29
identifier builtins which runtime symbols its own lowering declares in `callees`,
and calls the builtin allocating when one of those symbols is a pointer return
marked `noalias` in `codegen/runtime.ts`, which is that table's way of saying "a
fresh allocation per call". `nish_platform` returns a pointer and is deliberately
not `noalias`, so it stays out. That derived set must equal the one `escape.ts`
declares, and a callee the runtime table does not know is a failure too, because
it would otherwise read as "does not allocate". Then, for each builtin the signal
names, it generates a probe in the shape of `mem_getenv_scope` from the runtime
signature and asserts the emitted IR has no `nish_arena_release` before the `ret`.
No per-builtin fixture, so nothing to forget.

**An arrow-declared program and its `function` twin rewrite identically.** The
two spellings are the same program, so the differential rewriter owes them the
same JavaScript; it did not, which is how nine arrow-declared corpus programs
were compared with their builtins unrewritten. `arrow-parity.js` rewrites both
fixtures and compares them line by line, normalising only the declaration header
itself, and separately asserts both outputs reach the shim for all eleven members
the fixtures exercise — so two outputs that agree because the rewrite stopped
working for both spellings cannot pass.

Each guard was demonstrated against the broken state rather than assumed: the
first, with a tree whose set was cut back to the two file readers, names
`readdirSync` and `getenv` and fails both their probes; the second exits 1
against `git show 2806854^:tests/differential/rewrite.js` and 0 against the
current one.

Refs: src/codegen/escape.ts, tests/differential/rewrite.js
Tests: node tests/run.js allocating; node tests/differential/arrow-parity.js

* docs(std): add wp26-stdlib.md, the plan of record for the standard library

Every other subsystem here has a design note; `std/` had a README. The note
records the decisions the library already embodies, and three of them are worth
naming because the next module will face them:

**The line between a module and a builtin.** A builtin is for what the language
cannot express — a syscall, an operation the runtime must own for layout reasons,
or an effect the whole-program pass has to see. Everything expressible is a
module. `sort` is the live example: the budget has 194 bytes of headroom, so it
has to be answered in `std/` rather than in `runtime.c`.

**What the language's restrictions did to the API**, which is the part that
transfers: a function is never a value, so there is no `test(name, callback)`;
there is no `try`/`catch`, so an assertion records and *answers* a boolean,
because an out-of-range index panics and ends the process; there are no generics,
so there is one assertion per type; there are no optional parameters. The note
adds a sixth the library found rather than inherited — a module's private
functions share the importing program's flat symbol namespace, so a program with
its own `isBlank` cannot compile against `std/text`.

**Two claims in `std/README.md` that the code does not keep**, measured while
writing it: `std/text` references eight runtime symbols (the true claim is that
it added no *new* C function), and it does not compile under `--number-mode f64`
at all, because `s.length` and `charCodeAt` answer `number`. Spelling the widths
is necessary and not sufficient. The note carries a mode-by-mode table and
proposes the `tests/link/std_text_f64/` case that would have caught it; the fix
itself is not in this commit.

Refs: docs/wp21-packages.md, docs/wp23-language-surface.md

* feat(tests): close every gap between the Nish runner and the goldens it checks

The runner now covers section A rather than most of it. Over the corpus it went
from 600 checks with 6 skips to **1,106 checks with none**, in about five minutes.

The three sidecars it used to skip by name are implemented, and the third was the
interesting one. `.argv` is `splitWhitespace` onto the vector. `.stdout` needed
the compiler's own stdout, which `spawnSyncTo` can capture now — a dump flag
writes no IR, so such a case compares the dump and returns before the golden and
link work, and as a side effect the compiler's `wrote ...` chatter can no longer
land in the middle of the report. `.env` looked impossible, because the language
has no `setenv` and a child inherits this process's environment: POSIX `env(1)`
sets a child's variables without a shell, and `env -u` unsets one, so all three
forms of the sidecar are reachable — `NAME=value`, `NAME=` for empty-but-set, and
a bare `NAME` to unset. The `-u` flags come first, because `env` stops reading
options at its first operand, and a name repeated in the file takes its last line,
which is what assigning twice into the Node harness's object does. That the unset
form is real rather than incidentally passing is checkable:
`NISH_TEST_NOT_SET=leaked NISH_TEST_VALUE=wrong build/nish-runner io_getenv`
still passes.

Every emitted module is now assembled with `llvm-as` and verified with
`opt -passes=verify`, which is 444 of the new checks: the runner used to prove
the IR matched a golden but not that it was valid. The `tests/link/` programs are
walked too — `main.ts` discovery, the `args` flag file, `expected.err` as one
whole needle rather than a fragment per line, per-module goldens, `expected.ir`
substrings, then exit code and stdout — 53 more checks over 26 programs, 11 of
them negatives.

One `rm -rf` of the link output directory runs at startup, for a reason worth
stating: there is no unlink builtin, and a stale module from an earlier run would
otherwise be listed, verified and compared as though this run had emitted it. It
is the same "a POSIX utility stands in for the builtin" move as `env(1)`, and a
failure makes the link section one counted skip rather than a lie.

Every remaining skip is conditional and none fires on a machine with the
toolchain: a case with no golden, and one per missing tool. All five paths were
exercised by hiding tools and removing a golden.

Declined, and the header says so: the cross-module `declare`/`define` attribute
agreement, which needs a regular expression the language does not have, and
`UPDATE_GOLDENS`, which this runner must never do.

Measured: 1,106 checks, 0 failed, 0 skipped, 301 s over the corpus (was 600 / 6)
Tests: npm run test:nish; the `pop` subset in tests/run.js on every npm test

* fix(std): make the standard library mean one program in both number modes

`std/README.md` told a module author to spell the widths — `i32`, `i64`, `f64`,
never `number` — so that the module means the same thing under `--number-mode
f64`. `std/text` followed the rule and still did not compile in that mode at all:

    std/text.ts:154:10: error: Ternary branches must have the same type, got i32 and f64
      154 |   return left.length === right.length ? -1 : shorter;

Spelling your own widths is necessary and not sufficient. `s.length`, `a.length`
and `s.charCodeAt(i)` answer `number`, which *is* `f64` there, so
`let end: i32 = text.length` and `while (i < text.length)` are type errors — and
`indexOf` did not even error, because `f64 >= 0` type-checks, it just quietly
lowered differently. `std/testing` compiled in both modes but its `.length`
comparisons became `fcmp ogt double` in one of them.

Fourteen reads in `std/text` and two in `std/testing` now go through `toI32`, and
where a loop condition tests a length it is read **once** into an `i32` local
rather than converted per iteration — a string is immutable, so the local cannot
go stale. The default mode pays nothing: `toI32` on an `i32` is identity, so
`std/testing.ll` is byte-identical and `std/text.ll` has the same 627 instructions
it had before, trading a repeated load-and-truncate for one hoisted read. In f64
mode each converted read costs one `llvm.fptosi.sat.i32.f64`. stage1 compiles the
result to the same bytes as stage0, so the rule now holds for both compilers.

`tests/link/std_text_f64` is what stops the rule being prose again: an `args` file
of `--number-mode f64` and one assertion per function that used to be
mode-dependent. It also reaches both of `Suite`'s converted reads — `done` reads
`failures.length` on every run, and the detail line in `fail` only happens when a
check fails, so the case runs a second suite that fails on purpose and asserts its
exit code is 1 while its own stays 0.

The private helper `isBlank` is now `isTextBlankByte`, which is a rule and not a
whim: a function name is unique across the whole program whether exported or not,
and a `std/` module is compiled into its importer, so a helper called `isBlank`
stops any program declaring its own `isBlank` from compiling. `std/README.md`
carries both corrections — the width rule with its missing half, and naming a
private helper as though it were exported.

Refs: docs/wp26-stdlib.md §4, §3e
Tests: tests/link/std_text_f64, tests/link/std_text, tests/link/std_testing

* refactor(runtime): split the system-call half into runtime_os.c, with a ceiling each

Three new builtins pushed `runtime.c` from 4,154 to 4,670 bytes of `.text*` and
forced the ceiling up from 4,096 to 4,864 for the whole file. That is the wrong
coupling: the core runtime's budget should not move every time the language
reaches further into the operating system, and a reviewer asked exactly that
question about a standard library that had in fact cost it nothing.

The line is **whether the function's subject is the operating system**, which is
also the test for whether a builtin has to be C at all. `runtime_os.c` takes
`nish_exit`, the file I/O, `nish_is_dir`, `nish_mkdir`, the spawn family,
`nish_readdir`, `nish_monotonic_nanos`, `nish_getenv`, `nish_platform` and
`nish_arch`. `runtime.c` keeps what every program touches: the arena, strings,
number formatting, `nish_parse_number`, arrays and the panics. Three calls went
the other way on the same test and say so in the code: `nish_random`'s subject is
a pseudo-random sequence and its `time(0)` is a seed rather than the answer;
`nish_argv_init` makes no system call, because the entry point hands it `argc`
and `argv` and the work is `malloc` and `strcpy`; and `nish_platform` moved
despite making no call either, because its subject is the host and its branch
list grows when a platform is added. The moved code is byte-identical to what it
was, no symbol was renamed, and `runtime_os.c` includes `nish.h` rather than a
private copy of the prototypes, so the OS half compiles against the contract a C
host sees.

Two ceilings now, each the next 256-byte boundary above its measurement:

    runtime/runtime.c      3,480 of 3,584   (was 4,670 of 4,864)
    runtime/runtime_os.c   1,190 of 1,280

They sum to exactly the 4,670 of the single file, so nothing was gained or lost
in the move. The core's ceiling came **down**, and the two headrooms mean
different things on purpose: 104 bytes on a closed set that should only shrink,
and 90 on the OS half — less than one wrapper, `nish_readdir` being 294 — so the
next syscall builtin must raise that number in its own commit and can no longer
borrow room from the arena to hide in.

`scripts/build.sh` compiles `<dir>/runtime_os.c` whenever it is handed
`<dir>/runtime.c`, which is what keeps `nish --link` correct without touching
`src/index.ts` or `self/compile.ts`. The direct `clang` lines in `tests/run.js`
name both files instead, so a missed one is a link error rather than something a
script quietly repairs. `release.yml` now requires `runtime_os.c` in the tarball:
without that, a `files` regression could publish a compiler that links a program
printing a string and fails on any program that reads a file — the half of the
runtime whose absence a `hello.ts` smoke test cannot see.

The split costs nothing where it ships. `examples/hello.ts` and `examples/add.ts`
link byte-identically at both the size and speed profiles, which use LTO, and a
program that does list a directory is unchanged too. Without LTO it is still not
a regression: at `clang -O2` the linked `io_readdir` binary's `.text*` falls from
9,373 to 8,584 bytes, because `nish_readdir` stops carrying an inlined allocator.
On 4,000 `readdirSync` calls over a 37-entry directory the time is 41 ms either
way, inside a ±4 ms band: the work is in `getdents` and `strcmp`, not the bump
allocator.

Measured: runtime.c 3,480 of 3,584; runtime_os.c 1,190 of 1,280; hello.ts
byte-identical at both profiles; 41 ms either way on 152,000 directory entries
Refs: docs/wp7-runtime.md#runtime-additions-and-budget, docs/MASTER_PLAN.md §2
Tests: node tests/run.js budget; npm test (1301 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped);
npm run test:nish (1,114 checks, 0 failed, 0 skipped)

* fix(tests): create the directory the golden cases write into

Three cases — `io_files`, `io_mkdir`, `io_streams` — write into `build/test` by
that literal path. That directory is `tests/run.js`'s, and the Node harness
creates it before running anything, so the cases have always had it there. The
Nish runner created its own working directories and not that one, so on a clean
checkout those three failed at their first `writeFileSync` with
`golden cases: 1111 passed, 3 failed`.

It passed locally for as long as the runner has existed, because an earlier
`npm test` had left `build/test` lying around, and it failed the first time CI
ran the full pass on a fresh tree — which is the whole reason that job exists. A
green run on a dirty tree was proving less than it looked.

The runner now creates `build/test` with the reason written beside it, and the
full pass is 1,114 checks, 0 failed, 0 skipped starting from an empty `build/`.

Tests: rm -rf build && npm run test:nish

* docs(std): S1 landed without lifting the std/ naming rule

#57 gave every symbol a package scope, and `wp26-stdlib.md` pointed at the
heading that stated the blocker — which #57 renamed, because the namespace is no
longer flat. That broke the anchor and, more importantly, left the prose wrong:
it said the naming rule held "until S1 lands", implying S1 would lift it.

It does not. Package-scoped symbols key the whole-program fact table on a
package-qualified name, so two npm packages that each keep a private `helper()`
now compile together. A `std/` module is not a second package: a package is a
`node_modules/<name>/` directory and the root package's prefix is empty, so a
`std/` module shares its importer's package and the clash is unchanged. A
program that declares `isTextBlankByte` itself is still refused, with #57's own
wording — a function name must be unique across the program whether or not it is
exported. The rule is permanent until `std/` ships as its own package.

Refs: docs/wp21-packages.md

entries.title: call a C function with `declare function`
entries.body:
* feat(checker): call a C function with `declare function` (stage0)

WP27 S1, first half. A Nish program can now name a C function and call it:

```ts
declare function abs(n: i32): i32;
```

lowers to `declare i32 @abs(i32)` and a plain `call`. The spelling is
TypeScript's own ambient declaration, so the parser already accepts it and no
grammar was invented; the symbol is the identifier, which is the promise
`--emit-header` already makes in the other direction.

The declaration carries **no attributes**, because nothing about a body this
compiler cannot see is provable. The part that matters is what that does to
callers: `collectFacts` starts every function from the *pure* defaults and
discovers impurity by walking a body, so an absent body would have been read as
an empty one and marked every caller of a C function `readnone willreturn` —
a miscompile, not a missed optimisation. A foreign signature is therefore
seeded with the worst case and the fixpoint carries it outward. Measured on a
program with both kinds of caller: the function that calls C keeps only
`nounwind`, the one that does not keeps `nounwind willreturn readnone`, and the
impurity reaches `main` transitively.

S1 is scalars only, and that is the reason it is sound rather than a limitation
of it: with no pointer crossing the boundary there is nothing for escape
analysis to be wrong about. Widening the type check without revisiting the
escape story re-opens the class of the 0.1.0 `getenv` use-after-free, in user
code this time, so the block that seeds the facts says so.

One inherited proof stopped being true and is now a decision rather than an
assumption: `nounwind` is emitted unconditionally, justified by "the language
has no exceptions", and a C++ callee could unwind through a Nish frame.
Dropping it from every caller buys nothing, since a language with no `throw`
and no landing pad cannot act on an unwind it admits to, so S1 declares
unwinding out of a foreign call undefined — clang's own position compiling C —
and writes that next to the attribute.

Not done here, and the PR is not mergeable until it is: the `self/` mirror, so
stage1 emits the same bytes, plus the goldens, the `reject_*` cases, the
LANGUAGE.md rule and the cookbook entry.

Refs: docs/wp27-ffi.md

* fix(checker): keep the scalar predicate out of the interop import cycle

The previous commit reached `interop/abi.ts` for `isScalar` from the checker,
and that module imports `codegen/attributes.ts`, so
`checker/declarations -> interop/abi -> codegen/attributes -> emit/expressions`
closed a cycle. It failed at module initialisation rather than at a type error —
`ReferenceError: Cannot access 'stringBinaryEmitters' before initialization` —
which is why `tsc` was clean and `tests/self/support_oracle.js` was what caught
it.

Both directions of the C boundary ask the same question, but only one of them
can import that module: `--emit-header` runs after the whole program is
analysed, while a `declare function` is checked in pass 1. So the predicate
moves to `src/types.ts`, which owns the type model and which the checker already
imports, and `interop/abi.ts`'s `isScalar` delegates to it — one answer, no
cycle. The reason is written next to it so the next caller does not re-close the
loop.

Also regenerates the diagnostic registry the new rejections belong to; it is
generated rather than hand-kept, and `npm test` fails when it drifts (365
rules).

Tests: tests/self/support_oracle.js (879/879 lines agree)

* test(self): refresh the checked_self golden for the new registry rules

`self/codes.ts` is generated, so adding WP27's rejections moved `RULE_COUNT`
from 361 to 365 and pushed six declarations eight lines down. The golden records
what stage1 prints for `self/`'s own source, so it moves with the file.

Checked rather than accepted: the whole diff is that count and six line numbers
shifted by exactly the eight lines the four new rules added. `--update` will bake
a real regression into a golden just as willingly, so the diff is the evidence,
not the command.

* feat(self): mirror `declare function` into stage1, byte for byte

WP27 S1's second half. A construct enters `src/` and `self/` together, and the
IR oracle has no construct-level skip, so there was no landing this half-done.

`IR(stage0) == IR(stage1)` holds for an FFI program, `cmp`-clean, and all four
refusals agree between the two compilers word for word.

`declare` is a **contextual** keyword, matched by text next to `type`, `enum`,
`from` and `of` — so the lexer and `tests/lexer_oracle.js` are untouched, no
token needed renumbering inside the contiguous keyword range, and a variable may
still be called `declare`. The parser gives a foreign declaration the same four
children as a function with the empty node where the block goes, because
everything downstream indexes them positionally; `FunctionSig.body()` already
answered `null` for that shape, so the three body walkers needed nothing.

The purity hazard from the stage0 commit is here identically, and worth naming
rather than quietly fixing: a null body skips the fact collector, which leaves
`FunctionFacts` at its *pure* defaults, which would mark every caller of a C
function `readnone willreturn`. Seeded with the worst case in both compilers
now.

One bug found while mirroring. The stage0 half reused `interop/abi.ts`'s
`isScalar`, which leaves `i64` and `u64` out — but `cType` spells both
(`int64_t`, `uint64_t`), so that predicate would have refused a signature the
compiler can already write into a header. It had no other callers, so reusing it
was inheriting an unrelated exclusion rather than sharing a definition:
`isForeignScalar` now states the boundary on its own terms in both compilers and
`interop/abi.ts` is back to exactly what it was. Verified rather than reasoned:
`declare function labs(n: i64): i64` links against libc and `labs(-5)` is 5.

Tests: tests/cases/ffi_scalar (golden, native round trip), reject_ffi_body,
reject_ffi_export, reject_ffi_string_param, reject_ffi_string_return
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#calling-c, docs/wp27-ffi.md

* test: put FFI programs outside the differential oracle, with the reason

`tests/cases/ffi_scalar` calls libc's `abs`, the rewriter emits JavaScript that
references `abs`, the shim has no such export, and Node exits 1 where the native
binary exits 0.

Listed in `known-failures.txt`, and deliberately not fixed by teaching the shim
an `abs`: that would work and would teach the wrong lesson, because the next
program declares a different symbol. The oracle's premise is that one source
means the same thing in both worlds, and it does not hold for a source whose
meaning is "whatever this C function does". **Every FFI program is outside this
oracle by construction**, which is a real coverage cost of the feature rather
than an oversight, and it is recorded as one in `docs/wp13-differential.md` and
`docs/wp27-ffi.md` §5.

It is also why S1's evidence is arranged the other way round: a golden `.ll`, an
`llvm-as` pass, a native round trip against real libc, and the attribute
assertions the differential oracle could never have made anyway.

The `checked.txt` golden moves with the new cases, and its diff is the second
place the soundness property is now visible: both foreign functions dump
`effect=write willReturn=false readsMemory=true`, which is the seeding rather
than the pure defaults an absent body would otherwise have left.

* test: retire NL2125, whose rule this branch replaced

`#52` added `tests/wordings/`, which requires every code in the registry to be
provoked by some program or named in `unreachable.txt`. This branch deleted the
only message that reached NL2125 — `` `declare function` is not supported yet `` —
so two assertions failed at once: the case pinning NL2125 got the new
"must have no body" code instead, and NL2125 became provoked by nothing.

That is the coverage test working, and it caught something no other test in the
suite would have: a released diagnostic code left orphaned. The generator is
explicit that the number stays reserved — "a released compiler handed that number
to a rule, so it may never be handed to another one" — and `unreachable.txt`
already has a Retired section for exactly this.

So the case goes, because the rule it pinned no longer exists and its program now
provokes a better diagnostic, and NL2125 joins the retired list. The rules that
replaced it are pinned by `tests/cases/reject_ffi_*`, five cases whose wording
both compilers agree on.
