entries.title: add a rules card the compiler's own tests keep honest
entries.body:
* docs(cli): add a rules card the compiler's own tests keep honest

An AI writing a Nish program had nothing to read. The repository's agent
surface — `AGENTS.md`, `.claude/`, the `--json` contract — is all aimed at
someone working *on* the compiler, and the two documents aimed at someone
working *in* the language are the wrong shape for it: `docs/LANGUAGE.md` is
2,334 lines written to be browsed as a reference, and `runtime/nish.d.ts`
deliberately cannot express the flow rules it says `nish` is the authority on.

The failure mode that leaves is specific rather than general. A model trained
on TypeScript writes `xs.map(f)`, `if (xs.length)`, `throw`, `?.`, `x as T` and
a top-level `let` — code that parses, because the parser is TypeScript's, and
that `tsc --strict` accepts against the ambient declarations, and that this
compiler then rejects. The subset is much smaller than it looks, and nothing
said so in one pass.

`docs/AI.md` is that pass: the loop (`--json`, key on `code`, the exit codes)
first, then the roughly thirty TypeScript reflexes that get rejected with the
message each one produces, then types and the closed list of contexts a numeric
literal takes its width from, `Result`'s three rules, nullable narrowing,
declarations, statements, an exhaustive builtin inventory — inventing a method
is the most common way to write a program that does not compile, so the list
says what exists rather than describing it — memory, and recipes for `map`, a
tuple, a map, and shared behaviour without inheritance.

A digest written beside a reference is the kind of document that rots, and a
stale example teaches a rule the compiler no longer has. So the examples are
tests. Each fenced block carries a marker — `nish:ok`, `nish:ok-body`,
`nish:err NL2231`, `nish:err-body NL2188` — and `tests/run.js` compiles all
twenty on every run, asserting acceptance or that the expected code is among
the diagnostics. The expectation is the stable `code` and not the prose,
which is what the page tells its own reader to key on: a reworded message must
not fail this, and a renumbered rule must. Not one code here was written by
hand; each was read back from `--json` and pinned.

It ships. `docs/AI.md` and `llms.txt` join the `files` whitelist, so the rules
live beside the compiler an agent is driving rather than a fetch away, with no
version skew between them; the WP12 package check enforces both. `llms.txt`
indexes the two audiences separately, because sending someone writing a program
to `AGENTS.md` is the mistake this whole change is about.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md, AGENTS.md#machine-readable-surfaces
Tests: tests/run.js "docs/AI.md" section — 20 snippets compiled, each pinned to
  its diagnostic code; WP12 package whitelist; node docs/check-links.mjs

* docs(cli): let an agent merge its own pull request, except the release one

A pull request opened by an agent used to sit there. Nothing said what state it
had to be in before it went up, and nothing said who was supposed to merge it,
so the answer in practice was "a human, eventually" — which is a poor answer
when the change is finished, tested and unblocked, and nobody is actually
waiting to review it.

The rule now has two halves. A pull request **goes up finished**: `npm run
check` green, `npm test` green *and undegraded*, lint no worse than `main`, a
conventional title, and no conflict with `main` — merged and resolved before
pushing rather than left for a reviewer to find. "Undegraded" is the half worth
spelling out, because this suite skips rather than fails without LLVM 18 and a
green summary then looks identical to a run that proved everything; the skip
count decides what the run was worth, and only the two environmental skips (no
WASI sysroot, `NISH_BOOTSTRAP` unset) are expected.

Then **the agent merges it itself**, squashed, once CI is green on the current
head, no conflict remains, the suite really was run, and no human is requesting
changes or holding an unresolved thread. Until then it does not stop and does
not ask: it watches the pull request and works it toward that state — root-cause
the red check and push the fix, merge `main` in and resolve, implement the small
review asks — and merges when it arrives. Webhooks miss CI-success and
merge-state transitions, so that means re-checking on a schedule rather than
trusting events. The only thing that ends the loop without a merge is a blocker
it cannot clear alone, said once on the pull request.

The exception is the **Release PR**, and it is categorical rather than a
condition to weigh. `chore(release): <version>` on `release/next` is opened by
`release-pr.yml`, and merging it *is* the release: it tags, the tag dispatches
`release.yml`, and that builds the artifacts and publishes the tarball to npm.
None of that is undoable, and the pull request exists precisely so the release
notes get read before anyone else can read them. So an agent may prepare it and
say it is ready, and a human clicks merge — not because CI is red, but because
publishing is not a decision a green check makes.

That rule is written where it will actually be seen. `AGENTS.md` carries it in
full and `CLAUDE.md` in short, but `release-pr.yml` now also writes the warning
into the pull request body it generates, so it is on the Release PR itself
rather than only in a file an agent may not have opened. Documentation is still
guidance and not a lock: branch protection is what would enforce it, and that is
a repository setting rather than anything in this tree.

Refs: AGENTS.md#shipping-a-change-what-a-pull-request-must-be-and-who-merges-it,
  docs/wp12-release.md
Tests: npm test; node docs/check-links.mjs; all three workflow YAMLs parse; the
  generated release body rendered with dummy values to check the printf escaping

entries.title: key two generic rules on words only they contain
entries.body:
* fix(checker): key two generic rules on words only they contain

Two diagnostics were keyed wrongly, both for one reason:
`scripts/gen-diagnostic-codes.mjs` derives a rule's stable code from the
string literal written *at* the diagnostic call, and takes the longest
literal run of it.

**`NL3010` was answering for three rules that are not its own.** The
generic whole-program clash message was assembled as

    `Generic function \`${name}\` is also defined in ${file}; a function ` +
      "name must be unique across the program, and an instantiation is ..."

so the longest run of the literal the generator saw was
`` ` is also defined in ` `` — twenty-one characters that
`duplicate_export`, `duplicate_import` and `duplicate_internal` also
contain. All three carried `NL3010`. `code` is documented as a stable rule
identifier and `src/codes.ts` calls it a promise; a code that names four
unrelated rules is worse than no code for anything keying on it.

**The non-terminating-request rule had no code at all.** Its sentence was
built in a helper and returned, so the generator never saw it and it
carried `NL0000` despite having plenty of words of its own.

Both are now written as one literal at the call, and the helper returns the
four names the sentence interpolates rather than the sentence.
`nonTerminatingParts` says why in its own doc comment, and the two clash
sites say why they are one line. The sentences a user reads are unchanged,
byte for byte -- a concatenation and a single literal build the same string
-- so no golden, no `.err` and no parity comparison moves.

The ambiguous assignment is removed from the registry rather than left as a
retired entry, because a retired fragment stays in the table and keeps
matching: left there, `` ` is also defined in ` `` would have gone on
answering for the three. `NL3010` is handed to the rule it was meant for.
That number reached `main` an hour ago and has never been in a release, so
nothing outside this repository has ever seen it mean the other thing;
after 0.2.0 ships this correction would not be available.

Verified by running the diagnostics rather than by reading the table:

    duplicate_export     NL0000   (was NL3010)
    duplicate_import     NL0000   (was NL3010)
    duplicate_internal   NL0000   (was NL3010)
    a redeclared generic NL3010   "Generic function `dup` is also defined in ..."
    a growing request    NL2304   (was NL0000)

and mapping by mapping against `origin/main`: **0 moved**, 1 dropped (the
ambiguous fragment, deliberately), 2 added. Every other code keeps its
number.

`NL3010` needed a provoker of its own once it stopped borrowing three:
`tests/wordings/nl3010_generic_redeclared` declares `identity<T>` beside a
module that already does, and both compilers answer it the same way.
`NL2304` is provoked by `reject_generic_polymorphic_recursion`, which
already existed.

The uncoded backlog returns to **5**, the five whole-program messages that
were uncoded before WP18 landed, so `tests/run.js`'s pin holds without
being touched:

    stage0: 125/125 cases pin their code, coverage 321/380 codes,
            59 unreachable, uncoded=5
    stage1:  66/125 cases pin their code (46 refused by the parser,
            13 answered differently), coverage 223/380, uncoded=8

Refs: docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md
Tests: tests/wordings/nl3010_generic_redeclared, tests/cases/reject_generic_polymorphic_recursion

* docs(self): name the prefix trap G7 will walk into

An instantiation's symbol carries a package prefix (WP21 S1) and is minted
from the *instantiating* module's prefix. That is correct only because a
template may not yet be instantiated from another module, so the
instantiating module is always the declaring one and the two prefixes are
the same. G7 lifts exactly that refusal.

When it does, the prefix has to become the template's rather than the
caller's, or two packages importing one generic mint the same symbol and
the whole-program fact table -- keyed by symbol -- hands one instantiation
the other's purity and escape facts. That is a miscompile rather than a
link error, and it is the same failure WP21 S1 exists to prevent for plain
functions.

Written down beside G7 in the staged order, where whoever picks it up will
be standing, with `tests/link/package_generic` named as the fixture that
pins the prefix today and the one to extend.

Refs: docs/wp18-generics.md, docs/wp21-packages.md

entries.title: prove an index in range and emit no bounds check
entries.body:
* perf(checker): prove an index in range and emit no bounds check

WP15 §2.1 and §2.2. A new flow-sensitive analysis — `src/checker/bounds.ts`
and its mirror `self/bounds.ts` — decides for every `a[i]` and every
`s.charCodeAt(i)` whether the index is already known to be in range, and the
emitter writes the address and no check where it is. The checks that survive
now say so: §8's table row "bounds check not eliminated" ships with the
analysis, because a check that survives has to be able to explain itself.

The domain is five families of fact, all keyed by variable and never by a
property path, for the reason `narrowing.ts` gives — a local cannot be written
through an alias: `i >= 0`, `i < w.length`, `i <= w.length`, `i < n` and
`w.length >= n`. They come from the program as written: a literal initialiser,
a loop condition, an `if`, the right operand of `&&`, the statements after an
early exit, a hoisted `const n = xs.length`, an array literal of known size, a
sum of non-negative values, and — for the lower bound — an unsigned type,
which is the one *ranged* type the language already has.

What invalidates a fact is the whole soundness argument. An assignment to the
index drops its upper bounds and keeps the lower one only for an increment,
and only with `nsw`, because `--wrapping` *defines* the step past `INT_MAX` to
land on `INT_MIN`. Any call drops every array length fact, because a callee
holding the same array may `push`. A string's length cannot change once the
variable holding it is bound, so a string fact survives calls — which is the
whole reason a scanner's cursor comes out check-free with `isAlpha(...)`
sitting in the same loop condition. The walk is in evaluation order, so
`a[i] = f()` is judged against the facts that survive `f` and `f(a[i])`
against the facts before it, matching where the emitter writes each check.

The proof reaches `attributes.ts` as well: a proven access no longer lists
`nish_panic_index` as a callee, so a function whose every index is proven
keeps `willreturn`. Twenty-one goldens move, every one of them by losing a
compare, a branch, a cold block and a `noreturn` declaration.

The declared surface §2.1 proposed — `i: integer<0, 255>` — did not ship and
could not have: it needs a generic type parameter, which Phase 0 refuses and
which §9 item 8 owns, so the plan's own sequencing rules it out. A declared
range is one more source of facts for this domain when generics land, not a
second mechanism.

One guard changed, because the flag it guards now changes one more thing.
`--wrapping` *defines* the step past `INT_MAX` to land on `INT_MIN`, so the
proof may not carry a lower bound across an increment and a counted loop
compiled with it keeps the checks the default build removes. The old assertion
("removes every nsw and changes nothing else") is split into the two that are
now true and are stronger together: with `--unchecked-indexing` on both builds
the only difference is still `nsw` alone, and the checked `--wrapping` build
keeps `nish_panic_index` where the checked default build has none.
`docs/LANGUAGE.md` says so in both places the flag is specified.

Measured: 1.069x on the lexer-shaped cursor (630 ms against 673 ms of CPU, min of 15), against the 1.082x that removing every check buys on the same program — the hot function is byte-identical to the `--unchecked-indexing` build; a counted array loop is unchanged, worth the 0.5% §2b predicted
Refs: docs/wp15-performance.md §2.1, docs/LANGUAGE.md#element-access
Tests: tests/cases/arr_bounds_proven, str_bounds_proven, perf_bounds_loop, perf_bounds_quiet, arr_bounds_shrink_panic

* test(codegen): accept the proven index in the record-array golden

`arr_struct_contiguous` is WP15 §2a's case and its `.ll` was written before
§2.1/§2.2 existed. `ps[1]` on a two-element literal is provable, so the
merged compiler emits no length load, no `bounds.fail` block and no
`@nish_panic_index` declaration for it -- the two items compose, and an
index that is both a record slot and a proven one costs neither the pointer
chase nor the check.

The golden was regenerated rather than accepted on sight: the diff is 22
lines of check machinery removed and 0 added, the native round trip still
prints 17, and `llvm-as` and `opt -passes=verify` still accept the module.
`arr_struct_push_copy` is the control and is untouched -- its index is not
provable, and it keeps its check, which is what says the analysis
discriminated rather than swept.

The case comment now says the absence of the check is deliberate, so the
next reader does not read a missing `nish_panic_index` as a regression.

Tests: tests/cases/arr_struct_contiguous, arr_struct_push_copy

entries.title: import the runtime builtins from `nish:fs`, `nish:process` and `nish:io`
entries.body:
* feat(checker): import the runtime builtins from `nish:fs`, `nish:process` and `nish:io`

The builtins backed by the C runtime can now be imported by name instead of
reached for as globals:

```ts
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "nish:fs";
import { argv, exit } from "nish:process";
import { write, panic } from "nish:io";
```

`nish:` is the only bare specifier the language accepts, and it resolves to no
file. The import *renames a builtin the checker already has* rather than
introducing one: the call goes through the same rule, lowers to the same IR,
and `runtime.c` does not move a byte. The harness pins that — it compiles
`io_nish_import` and `io_nish_import_global` and compares the two bodies, so a
lowering that ever came to depend on which spelling a program used would show
up as a diff rather than as a surprise.

The reason to prefer an import is the name, not the code it emits. A global
builtin is consulted only when no user function of that name is in scope, so
declaring `panic` silently replaces it and nothing says so. Declaring one that
collides with an import is an error at the import instead.

`as` works, and that is what made the checker record which builtin each local
name stands for: the emitter dispatches builtins on the identifier's own text,
and under an import that text is whatever the program chose to call it.
Diagnostics still name the canonical rule, so `exit(1, 2)` reports
`process.exit`; `exit` terminates control flow exactly as `process.exit` does;
and `argv`, `platform` and `arch` keep their kind, so calling one is refused.

Everything else stays global — `Math.*`, the width conversions, `console.log`,
`Arena.*`, `Ok` and `Err`. They lower to an LLVM intrinsic or a single
instruction and cost no runtime at all, so they read as language rather than
as library, and an import would only add ceremony.

Nothing migrates. The global spellings are unchanged and still legal, `self/`
still uses them, and the two compilers gained the feature together: they agree
byte for byte on the IR and on every diagnostic, spans included.
`runtime/nish.d.ts` declares the three modules, so `tsc --strict` and an editor
accept the imports as well.

Measured: runtime.c unchanged at 4,088 of its 4,096-byte `.text` budget; the imported and global spellings emit identical IR
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#builtin-modules-nish
Tests: tests/cases/io_nish_import, tests/cases/io_nish_rename, tests/cases/reject_nish_unknown_module

* fix(self): stage1 missed the builtins a `nish:` import renamed

Three bugs the new cases turned up, none of which a golden alone would have
caught.

**stage1's attribute pass keyed on the identifier's text**, so a call to `exit`
imported from `nish:process` looked like no call at all: `io_nish_rename` came
out `willReturn=true` with `callsNoReturn=false` and no `nish_exit` among its
callees — a `willreturn` on a function that does not return, which is a wrong
attribute rather than a cosmetic difference. Both callee-fact helpers now take
the canonical name, the way stage0's dispatch already did. The two other rules
that read the spelling rather than the binding went the same way: an imported
`exit` did not terminate control flow, so a `main` ending on one was rejected,
and an imported `argv` escaped the read-only rule that refuses `argv[0] = x`
and `argv.push(...)`.

**The differential harness never descended into an arrow-function body.** Its
"top-level `const` folds to its value" branch matches
`export const main = (): number => { ... }` too — that is how the language
spells a function since WP22 — and returned the declaration without visiting
its initialiser. Every arrow-form program in the corpus was therefore compared
as plain TypeScript: no `| 0` wrapping, no shim call, no Nish semantics at all.
It is pre-existing and has nothing to do with builtin modules; these are simply
the first arrow-form programs in the corpus that call an identifier builtin.
Fixing it surfaced no other divergence — 142 of 152 programs agree and the
remaining ten are the documented ones.

**The rewriter did not know `nish:` imports**, and left the specifier standing
for Node to resolve. It now drops the statement and resolves each local name
through the canonical map, so an `as` rename reaches the shim helper its global
spelling would.

The stage1 goldens are regenerated with it, and record the invariant directly:
`io_nish_import` and `io_nish_import_global` carry identical facts and identical
callee lists, and `io_nish_rename` carries `willReturn=false` with `nish_exit`.

Measured: 142/152 differential programs agree with Node, 0 unexpected; stage0 and stage1 agree byte for byte on the IR and the checked dump of all three cases
Tests: tests/cases/io_nish_rename, tests/self/goldens/checked.txt

* feat(cli): import the standard library as `nish/<module>`

`std/` is reached by its package specifier instead of by a path up the tree:

```ts
import { Suite } from "nish/testing";
import { trim } from "nish/text";
```

`nish/<module>` resolves to `std/<module>.ts` beside the running compiler
rather than relative to the importing file, so the same specifier works at any
depth and from outside this repository. What arrives is ordinary Nish source —
compiled into the program that imports it, seen by the whole-program attribute
pass, inlined or specialised or dropped on the same terms as a local function.
A module imported and never called is dropped whole: measured at the `speed`
and `size` profiles, which link with `-flto -Wl,--gc-sections`, a program
importing three `std/text` functions and calling none is byte-identical to the
same program without the import.

**This is WP21's first slice, not a detour around it.** `std/README.md` refused
to fake a bare specifier because a resolver that special-cased the directory
would be a second module system, and §5b said bare specifiers are rejected.
That reasoning holds for third-party packages, which are still refused. It does
not hold for the compiler's own package, for two reasons true only of it: there
is exactly one correct `std/` for a given compiler, because the two are one
package and cannot be skewed against each other; and it is the answer Node
gives, now that `package.json` declares `"./*": "./std/*.ts"` — `nish/text` is
a package self-reference, `import.meta.resolve` answers `std/text.ts`, and
`tsc` under `moduleResolution: node16` resolves it to the same file, which is
what gives an editor go-to-definition into the real source. The compiler
short-circuits to that answer instead of walking `node_modules` to reach it.
Both documents now say so rather than being quietly contradicted.

The specifier prefixes moved to `branding.ts` on both sides, where §2 says the
package's own name belongs. That also closes a hole the `nish:` scheme opened
when it landed with the name hardcoded in two module tables.

One divergence the parity gate would have caught: stage1 derives its package
root from `argv[0]`, so it resolved `./build/../std/text.ts` where stage0
resolved `std/text.ts`. A module's resolved path is its identity *and* the name
in its IR header, so that was a byte the gate compares; normalising it makes
all three modules of the new link case byte-identical from both compilers.

The three existing `std_*` link cases keep their relative imports on purpose:
that form still works and is still guaranteed, and those cases are what prove
it.

Measured: a `std/text` import that is never called costs 0 bytes at the speed and size profiles (4,648 with and without); stage0 and stage1 emit byte-identical IR for all three modules of tests/link/std_bare_specifier
Refs: docs/wp21-packages.md#5b, std/README.md
Tests: tests/link/std_bare_specifier, tests/cases/reject_std_unknown_module, tests/cases/reject_bare_package

* fix(self): keep `process.argv` out of the path library

`packageRoot()` went into `self/paths.ts` when `nish/<module>` needed it, and
that broke nine modules: it reads `process.argv[0]`, which the language allows
only in a program with an entry `main`, and `tests/run.js` compiles every
`self/` module on its own. `paths.ts` and the eight modules importing it stopped
compiling standalone with "`process.argv` requires a `main` entry point".

The check was right about more than the test. A path library has no business
reading the command line, and the rule that caught it — `argv` exists only
where an entry wrapper built it — is the same rule stated a different way. So
the root goes back to the driver, which is the one place `process.argv` is
legal, and travels as `Options.packageRoot`; `stdModulePath` and
`stdModuleNames` take it as a parameter instead of reaching for it.

An empty root, which is what the driver answers when it can find neither
`scripts/build.sh` beside the binary nor one in the working directory, makes
`nish/x` resolve to nothing and report itself as a module the library does not
have. That is the same answer as before and the right one: there is no library
to import from.

Tests: every `self/` module compiles standalone again; tests/link/std_bare_specifier

* test(cli): provoke NL2312, the imported-builtin-as-a-type refusal

Every code in the registry has to be provoked by a case under `tests/wordings/`
or excused in `unreachable.txt`, and NL2312 was neither: the message existed,
the generator gave it a number, and nothing ever triggered it.

The shape matters more than it looks. Naming the import in a *variable*
annotation does not reach the diagnostic — `importsUsedAsTypes` is filled in
lazily while bodies are checked, and the refusal is raised in pass 1b, before
that. A *parameter* type resolves during signature collection, which is early
enough. `nl2073_function_as_type` makes the same move for an imported function,
so this case is its twin for a builtin one.

Tests: tests/wordings/nl2312_builtin_import_as_type

* docs(cli): keep the §5b anchor, and correct WP26 on resolving `nish/`

Two things the CI lint job caught that the test suite cannot: it runs
`docs/check-links.mjs`, and nothing local had.

Amending §5b of wp21 in its *heading* changed that heading's anchor, and
`wp26-stdlib.md` links to it. A heading other documents link to is an interface,
so the heading goes back to what it was and the amendment moves to the first
line of the body, where it reads the same and breaks nothing.

The link led to the second thing. `wp26-stdlib.md` is the plan of record for
`std/` and still said the library "is not resolvable by name", with the same
"deliberately not faked" reasoning `std/README.md` carried before this branch
changed its mind. It is resolvable now, so that bullet said the opposite of what
the compiler does. It now says what the other two notes say, and why the
argument that held for third-party packages does not hold for the compiler's
own.

* test(cli): renumber the imported-builtin-as-a-type case to NL2313

The wordings harness reads the expected code out of the filename, and merging
main moved this message one place along the `NL2xxx` band — `expected NL2312,
got NL2313`. The case is unchanged; only its name and the comment naming the
code are.

Worth knowing for the next one: a wordings case is pinned to a number that a
merge can move, so adding a diagnostic on a branch means re-checking its code
after every merge that touches the same band, not only after the one that
introduced it.

entries.title: add std/json, and check the CLI contract from a harness in Nish
entries.body:
`std/` gains a third module and `tests/nish/` a second program. `std/json`
answers the value of one field of one flat JSON object — a reader and not a
parser: string values come back unescaped, everything else as the bytes it was
written with, an absent field as `null`, and nothing is validated.
`tests/nish/cli.ts` is why it exists. That harness is a Nish program reading
the compiler's own output and checking the contract `AGENTS.md` and
`docs/wp12-release.md` state: `--help` on stdout with exit 0 against the same
text on stderr with exit 2, every advertised flag named in the usage, one flat
`--json` object per diagnostic carrying a stable `code` and the `severity` a
tool filters on, the dump flags answering on stdout without writing IR, and
each documented exit-code band — 0, 1, 2, 3 and 70 — driven from outside the
compiler.

It is not a second implementation of the WP12 block in `tests/run.js`. That
promise is made *to a program that reads the output*, and until now no such
program existed here. The harness takes the name and version it expects from
`package.json` with the same `jsonField`, so a release cannot leave the
expectation behind, and it runs against a self-hosted compiler as readily as
against stage0 — 69 checks green on `dist/index.js`, 57 with 2 declared skips
on `build/nish`, which the bootstrap CI job now runs. `npm test` runs it in
full rather than over a subset, because it spawns eighteen compilers rather
than four hundred.

It pins the shape and not the bytes, because the shape is what both compilers
promise and writing the checks against stage0's sentences would have made this
a second place to edit whenever a message improves. Two things that came out
of pointing it at stage1: `--json`'s stdout carries objects and nothing else —
the `wrote <file>` progress line is on stderr, which `AGENTS.md` described as
"nothing on stderr" and now describes correctly — and stage1's driver still
calls itself `compile` in its usage text, which is a counted skip here and the
same note `tests/run.js` already carries.

`std/testing` grew the three assertions `tests/nish/run.ts` had written by
hand and the new harness needed as well: `contains` for a fragment of a
captured stream, `containsAll` for an expectation file with one fragment per
line, and `eqLines`, which reports the first differing line of a generated
text against a golden rather than printing both. The golden runner now calls
them and is 53 lines shorter for it, and `tests/link/std_testing_fail` pins
the wording of each new failure message.

Two checks came with the library growing. `npm pack` must ship every
`std/*.ts` in the tree rather than the two a written list happened to name,
which answers `docs/wp26-stdlib.md` §7 question 6 by asking the tree instead
of a list; and `tsc --strict` must accept `std/` and both harnesses against
`runtime/nish.d.ts`, beside the corpus and `self/` — `std/` is the code a user
imports, so the claim that a program nish accepts is never one tsc refuses is
worth as much there as on the corpus.

Merging `main`'s `nish/<module>` resolver in also required three statements
about `std/` to be made true again: stage1's literal module list, the
`reject_std_unknown_module` case that used `nish/json` as its example of a
module the library does not have, and the copy of that diagnostic in
`docs/LANGUAGE.md`.
metrics: 1534 passed, 0 failed, 2 skipped (the two environmental ones); the CLI contract is 69 checks against stage0 and 57 with 2 declared skips against the self-hosted compiler

entries.title: let a construct be implemented once, in `self/`
entries.body:
Every construct since S5 has been written twice, and none of the gates
required it. Two mechanical things did: `tests/run.js` compiles a case
with stage0, so a construct stage0 lacks can have no golden `.ll`; and
the oracles read a case stage0 refuses as a silent skip, so a construct
landing in `self/` alone would quietly shrink the comparison rather than
declare that it had.

`tests/self/stage1_only.txt` is the register that ends both. A named
case is compiled by a stage1 binary the seed builds, and its golden,
`llvm-as` pass and native round trip are stage1's; the oracles and
`parity.js` count it as declared rather than skipped; `nish-cmp.js`
expects the seed to refuse it until the release that has the construct.
`stage1_probe` is the fixture that keeps the path walked.

`tests/self/seed.js` gives the four oracles that outlive stage0 one seed
resolution — `--seed`, then `NISH_BOOTSTRAP`, then `build/nish` — so
none of them links its subject with `dist/index.js` any more, which is
G2.3. Two hidden stage0 dependencies went with the builder.

Nine compiler fixes came out of the wording work, seven of them one
compiler accepting what the other refuses: a constant and a function of
one name; a `for...of` head with two declarators, an annotation or an
initializer; `new C<T>()` on a declared class; an i64/u64 literal past
2^53; a void ternary; three clash messages and `++` on a string; and
stage0 quoting the cooked literal under a caret pointing at the source.

`tests/self/parity.js` rebuilds its stage1 every run — it reused
`build/self/compile` when the file existed, so the gate could report
green against a compiler nobody rebuilt. The corpus half of that gate
is now a nightly workflow, and `scripts/smoke.sh` is off `mapfile`.
